terms.definition: A record that something happened, named in the past tense, such as "OrderPlaced".
A producer emits events; a consumer reacts to them. The producer does not call the consumer directly.
The producer emits an event and moves on, rather than waiting for the reaction to finish.

before.note: Read Publish-Subscribe first: event-driven architecture is built on the fan-out it describes, and the delivery and ordering rules there carry over. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: In a request-driven system, a service makes something happen by calling another service and waiting. In an event-driven system, a service instead announces that something happened and moves on. AWS describes it as using events to trigger and communicate between decoupled services, with three key components: event producers, event routers, and event consumers. A producer publishes an event to the router, which pushes it to consumers [[aws-eda]].

The payoff is decoupling. Because producer and consumer services are separated by the router, they can be scaled, updated, and deployed independently [[aws-eda]]. Microsoft frames the same style around event producers that generate a stream of events, event consumers that listen for them, and event channels, often implemented as event brokers, that transfer events from producers to consumers [[ms-eda]].

This is the next step up from publish-subscribe. Pub-sub is the mechanism that fans one message out to many subscribers; event-driven architecture is what you design once the things on the stream are facts about the business, not commands aimed at a particular service. The shift from "call this service" to "announce this fact" is the whole idea.

terms.definition: A design where decoupled services communicate by producing and reacting to events through a router or channel.
A service that publishes an event when something happens, without knowing who consumes it.
The broker or ingestion layer that carries events from producers to consumers.
A service that reacts to events it subscribes to, on its own schedule.

stages.name: How it works
body: The strongest form of event-driven design makes the event log the source of truth. Microsoft's Event Sourcing pattern says that instead of storing only the current state, you store the full series of actions on an object in an append-only store, and that this store serves as the system of record, the authoritative source for the current state. Each entity has its own ordered event stream recording every change to it [[ms-event-sourcing]].

Because the events are kept rather than overwritten, current state is something you compute from the events: applications derive the current state of an entity by replaying all the events in its stream, a process the page calls rehydration, and they can read the history of events at any point. Microsoft contrasts this with the usual create-read-update-delete model, where an application reads data, modifies it, and updates the current state, typically using transactions that lock the data [[ms-event-sourcing]].

On top of this log, consumers can build their own views. The page says applications typically implement materialised views, and that the log gives the flexibility to build new read models from historical events without changing the write side [[ms-event-sourcing]]. The pub-sub fan-out you already know is what delivers each event to every subscription, and the producer never has to know those consumers exist.

terms.definition: A store you only add to, never overwrite, so the full history of changes is kept.
The ordered sequence of events for one entity, recording every change to it.
The authoritative source of truth; in event sourcing, the event store itself.
Recomputing current state, or a view, by reading the event stream again from an earlier point.

reading.what: Why storing the full series of actions in an append-only store makes the log the system of record that you replay to derive state.
How an event router gives one central place to audit and set policies on who can publish and subscribe.

canNow: Explain what event sourcing stores and why.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The first hard problem is publishing an event reliably. If a service writes its database row and then publishes the event as a separate step, one can succeed while the other fails, so a committed change emits no event, or a rolled-back change emits one. Microsoft's Transactional Outbox pattern avoids this by saving the events in an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business object, which guarantees no data loss; a separate worker then queries the outbox for unhandled entries, publishes them to the broker, and marks them processed [[ms-outbox]].

The second is that events can arrive more than once, so consumers have to be safe to repeat. The outbox guidance says guaranteed delivery of events is an important part of supporting idempotent message processing [[ms-outbox]]. In our own words, a consumer must handle the same event twice with the same effect, and one way to do that is to record the ids of events it has already processed.

A related pattern is CQRS, which Microsoft describes as separating read and write operations into separate data models. Microsoft advises that commands should represent specific business tasks, such as "Book hotel room" rather than "set status to reserved", which captures intent and aligns the commands with business processes. In our own words, in an event-driven system those commands can produce events, and the read side can be a projection built from them [[ms-cqrs]].

terms.definition: Writing to the database and the broker as two steps that can disagree, losing or inventing events.
Saving the event in an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then shipping it separately.
Handling the same event twice with the same effect as once, needed under at-least-once delivery.
Separating write commands from read queries, so the read side can be a projection built from events.

reading.what: How writing the event in the same transaction removes the dual-write risk, and how it supports idempotent processing.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Event-driven design buys loose coupling and independent scaling, but it changes when things are "done". Because the producer returns after publishing and consumers react later, the system is eventually consistent: a reader may not reflect the change the instant the producer finishes. Microsoft's event-driven page says the style might not suit workloads where business transactions require strong consistency across services, or where simple request-response workflows with synchronous calls meet your latency and throughput needs [[ms-eda]]. A question that needs an immediate answer, such as whether stock exists at checkout, still needs a direct call.

It also adds operational surface. Microsoft's event-driven page lists the operational overhead of event brokers and asynchronous error handling [[ms-eda]]. In our own words, each consumer also has its own backlog that can fall behind, and following a flow means tracing it across several services rather than reading one call stack. Microsoft's event sourcing page calls the pattern complex, says it constrains future design decisions in the parts of the system that use it, and says to adopt it when benefits such as auditability justify the complexity [[ms-event-sourcing]].

So the pattern fits where decoupling, auditability and replay are worth that price: many independent reactions to the same facts, pipelines that aggregate or transform streams, and systems that must add new consumers without touching producers. Where a simple synchronous call would do, a plain request is still the right tool. AWS calls it common in modern applications built with microservices, and says decoupled services can be scaled, updated and deployed independently [[aws-eda]].

terms.definition: Readers converge on the producer's state some time after the event, not instantly.
A read model built from the event stream, rebuildable by replaying it.
Unprocessed events waiting for a consumer; a consumer that falls behind has a growing backlog.
The work of reconstructing state from events, which event sourcing trades for its auditability and flexibility.

misconceptions.myth: An event is just an asynchronous way to call a specific service.
misconceptions.truth: An event is a fact that any number of consumers may react to; the producer does not name or know its consumers [[aws-eda]].

misconceptions.myth: Writing the row and publishing the event separately is fine.
misconceptions.truth: The two can disagree; the outbox pattern saves the event in the same transaction to guarantee no data loss [[ms-outbox]].

misconceptions.myth: Event sourcing just means logging what happened.
misconceptions.truth: The event store is the system of record, and current state is rebuilt by replaying the stream, not stored directly [[ms-event-sourcing]].

misconceptions.myth: Once the producer publishes, the whole operation is finished.
misconceptions.truth: Consumers react later. The event sourcing page says projections built by replaying events are only eventually consistent, and the event-driven page says the style might not suit business transactions that need strong consistency across services [[ms-event-sourcing]] [[ms-eda]].

tryIt.intro: These use the command-line tools that ship with Apache Kafka against a local or test cluster, to see events as an append-only log. They are the commands from the Kafka quickstart: the topic name quickstart-events is the page's own, and each line you type into the producer becomes one event. The page shows its own output; yours depends on your cluster.

commands.warning: This creates a topic on the cluster at localhost:9092. Run it only against a test or local cluster.

commands.shows: Appends events: by default each line you enter is written as a separate event. Stop it with Ctrl-C.
commands.warning: This writes events to the topic. Run it only against a test or local cluster.
